title: HAZOP basics
ends: You can chair the next HAZOP.

steps.q: In a HAZOP, what is a deviation made of?
board: In a HAZOP, what is a
steps.title: Deviations
steps.summary: A HAZOP deviation is a guide word combined with a process parameter: 'no' + flow gives no flow, 'more' + pressure gives high pressure. Parameters include flow, pressure, temperature, level and composition; guide words include no, more, less, reverse and other than. The team works through each section of the process and every sensible deviation.

opts.t: A guide word plus a parameter

steps.q: The deviation is 'high pressure in the reactor'. What does the team write down next?
steps.title: The HAZOP row
steps.summary: A HAZOP row runs deviation, causes, consequences, safeguards, actions. For high reactor pressure the team first lists causes, such as cooling failure, a blocked vent or fast dosing, then the consequences if nothing intervenes, then the existing safeguards. If they are not enough, an action is recorded with an owner and a date.

steps.q: Which is usually the strongest safeguard against reactor overpressure?
steps.title: Safeguard strength
steps.summary: Alarms depend on someone noticing and acting in time, and procedures depend on people following them every time. A relief valve or bursting disc sized for the specific overpressure case works without human action, so it is usually the strongest safeguard. Count a safeguard only if it is independent of the cause and is sized and tested for that case.

opts.t: A warning sign on the reactor

draw: alarm → needs a person, in time

steps.q: When should a new plant's HAZOP be done?
steps.title: Timing
steps.summary: A plant HAZOP is done when the P&IDs are firm but before construction, when changes are still cheap on paper. A lighter review such as a what-if study is useful at the concept stage, and the HAZOP should be revisited whenever the plant changes and periodically every few years.

draw: revisit on change, every few years

steps.q: Who should be in a HAZOP team?
board: Who should be in a HAZOP
steps.title: The team
steps.summary: A HAZOP team is cross-functional: process, operations, instrumentation, maintenance and safety, plus a chemist for batch processes. Operators are especially valuable because they know how the plant is really run. An independent, trained chair keeps the team on the method, and a scribe records every row.

steps.q: You want to swap the reaction solvent for a cheaper one. Does that need a hazard review?
steps.title: Change = review
steps.summary: Changing a solvent changes flash point, boiling point, toxicity and static behaviour, and can affect heat removal, the relief case and the reaction itself. It must go through management of change, with a hazard review (often a focused HAZOP) before the first batch, followed by updated procedures and training.

opts.t: Only if the price changes a lot

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: HAZOP, the meeting where we ask what could go wrong, before it does. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read HAZOP made practical next.

q1.text: Question 1. In a HAZOP, what is a deviation made of?

q1-r1.text: Those come next. First you need the deviation itself.

q1-r2.text: Alarms and trips are safeguards. Later in the row.

q1-r3.text: Scores come later, if at all. Start with what can deviate.

q1-b0.text: Take a parameter: flow, pressure, temperature, level, composition.

q1-b1.text: Add a guide word: no, more, less, reverse, other than.

q1-b2.text: Together they make a deviation. No plus flow is no flow. More plus pressure is high pressure.

q1-b3.text: The team walks every line and vessel, one section at a time, through each deviation that makes sense.

q2.text: Question 2. The deviation is 'high pressure in the reactor'. What does the team write down next?

q2-r0.text: Safeguards come after you know what you're guarding against.

q2-r1.text: Actions are last. You haven't found the problem yet.

q2-r2.text: Causes first. What could make the pressure go high?

q2-r3.text: Cost isn't a HAZOP column. Not yet, anyway.

q2-b0.text: Each row follows the same order.

q2-b1.text: Causes: what could push the pressure up? Cooling failure, a blocked vent, or dosing too fast.

q2-b2.text: Consequences: what happens if nothing stops it? Then the safeguards already in the design.

q2-b3.text: If the safeguards aren't enough, the team writes an action, with a name and a date.

q3.text: Question 3. Which is usually the strongest safeguard against reactor overpressure?

q3-r0.text: An alarm needs a person to see it and act in time.

q3-r1.text: Procedures help, but people skip steps on a bad night.

q3-r2.text: Yes! It works without anyone touching it.

q3-r3.text: A sign won't hold back the pressure.

q3-b0.text: An alarm only works if someone sees it, understands it and acts in time.

q3-b1.text: A procedure depends on people following it every time, even on night shift.

q3-b2.text: A relief valve or bursting disc, sized for that exact case, works on its own, discharging to a safe place.

q3-b3.text: Count a safeguard only if it's independent of the cause, and actually sized and tested for that case.

q4.text: Question 4. When should a new plant's HAZOP be done?

q4-r0.text: After start-up, changes cost ten times more. And it's late.

q4-r1.text: Right! Firm enough to review, early enough to change.

q4-r2.text: Without drawings, there's nothing to walk through.

q4-r3.text: That's an investigation, not a HAZOP.

q4-b0.text: Too early, and there's nothing firm to review. Too late, and every change means cutting steel.

q4-b1.text: The sweet spot is when the P and I Ds are firm but before construction. Changes are still cheap on paper.

q4-b2.text: A smaller review, often a what-if, is useful earlier at the concept stage.

q4-b3.text: And the HAZOP must be revisited when the plant changes, and every few years.

q5.text: Question 5. Who should be in a HAZOP team?

q5-r0.text: One person can't see all the ways a plant goes wrong.

q5-r1.text: Safety alone doesn't know the process or the instruments.

q5-r2.text: Yes! Many eyes, and a chair with no stake in the design.

q5-r3.text: Rank speeds up sign-off, not hazard-finding.

q5-b0.text: Process, operations, instrumentation, maintenance, safety, and a chemist for batch processes.

q5-b1.text: Operators matter a lot. They know how the plant is really run.

q5-b2.text: The chair should be independent and trained, keeping the team on the method and the clock.

q5-b3.text: Plus a scribe to record every row, so nothing gets lost.

q6.text: Question 6. You want to swap the reaction solvent for a cheaper one. Does that need a hazard review?

q6-r0.text: Only a solvent? Flash point, toxicity, reactivity... all new.

q6-r1.text: Yes! Anything that isn't like-for-like goes through MOC and a hazard review.

q6-r3.text: After the first batch is too late to find out.

q6-b0.text: A new solvent brings a new flash point, boiling point, toxicity and static behaviour.

q6-b1.text: It can change heat removal, the relief case, and even the reaction itself.

q6-b2.text: So it goes through management of change: a hazard review, often a focused HAZOP, before the first batch.

q6-b3.text: Then update the procedures and train the people. More in HAZOP made practical on pharmacheme dot in.
